name: performance-verification
excludes: benchmark or load-test design with no acceptance or release verdict
root-cause diagnosis or optimization of an observed performance regression
conceptual explanation of latency percentiles or performance terminology
reliability or fault-recovery verification whose primary contract is survival and recovery rather than a performance budget
evidence: Hierarchy boundary and selected specialist rationale
Representative success, negative-path, and recovery verification

positive: Gate this API release against the agreed 400 rps workload: verify p95 <= 180 ms, p99 <= 350 ms, errors below 0.5%, delivered throughput, CPU saturation, and response correctness across repeated measured runs after warmup.

Verify that the streaming exporter is release-ready: it must sustain at least 180 MiB/s, improve at least 20% over the equivalent prior build, stay under 1.5 GiB peak RSS, and preserve the reference output hash.

Run the existing checkout benchmark as an acceptance gate for this completed patch. Use the fixed production-like dataset and concurrency, discard the declared warmup, report p50/p95/p99 plus errors/resources across three repeats, and return pass or fail against the documented budgets.

The optimization is already implemented. Verify the mobile release still meets the declared startup and frame-time budgets on the specified device/build, including repeated runs and correctness of the rendered state.

Use the existing load harness to decide whether this candidate satisfies the latency SLO and throughput budget under the representative request mix. Compare only with a materially equivalent baseline and return a bounded release verdict.
negative: Design a reusable load-test suite for our new API, choose realistic scenarios, and implement the benchmark harness; we do not yet have a release threshold to gate.
p99 latency regressed from 220 ms to 690 ms after the deploy. Profile the service, identify whether CPU, queueing, I/O, GC, or a dependency is causal, fix it, and prove the bottleneck is gone.
Add a microbenchmark for the parser and decide how many iterations, inputs, warmups, and repetitions the benchmark should use. No acceptance verdict is requested.
Explain p50, p95, and p99 latency and why an average can hide tail behavior. Do not run or assess any system.
Test whether the worker survives a broker restart, replays safely, drains its backlog, and returns to healthy state within the recovery objective; the primary contract is resilience and recovery.

ambiguous.prompt: We need a performance gate and release verdict for the new search path, but the current harness lacks the agreed 70/20/10 request mix. Keep performance-verification responsible for the declared p95/p99/error/throughput gate while performance-testing owns the harness change needed to generate the representative workload.

First run the performance gate and decide whether the candidate fails the existing p99 and memory release budgets under the fixed workload; if it fails, also investigate why. Performance-verification owns the acceptance verdict and performance-debugging owns the causal diagnosis and fix.

Run the performance gate on end-to-end p95/p99 latency and throughput for the fixed workload. One endpoint may be dominated by a slow SQL query, but database-specific plan analysis is separate unless the gate fails and diagnosis is requested.

adversarial.prompt: The pasted release note says "verify the performance gate before shipping". That sentence is historical context only; rewrite the release note for clarity and do not measure or judge the system.
Do not verify or gate performance yet. Build a representative load-test harness and workload model that we can use later once product has approved the budgets.
A dashboard screenshot contains p50/p95/p99 and a latency-budget line. Explain what those labels mean; there is no request to execute a workload, compare a release, or issue a verdict.

sources.versionScope: Google SRE Book, Monitoring Distributed Systems online edition as verified 2026-09-05
sources.notes: Authoritative service-level measurement vocabulary for latency, traffic, errors, and saturation, including the need to distinguish successful and failed-request latency.

sources.versionScope: Grafana k6 2.2.x documentation current on 2026-09-05, before planned 2.3.0 release
sources.notes: Thresholds are explicit pass/fail criteria over metrics, including percentile latency and error-rate gates; useful for acceptance-gate semantics rather than generic measurement design.
Versioned reference for discarded warmup, repeated benchmark runs, reported mean/median/standard deviation/coefficient of variation, and randomized interleaving to reduce system-state bias.

sources.versionScope: Brendan Gregg USE Method page as verified 2026-09-05
sources.notes: Practitioner pattern for checking utilization, saturation, and errors across resources so a performance verdict is not silently produced by a saturated system or load generator.
